q: The alcohols may be considered as derivatives of alkanes.
e: Alcohols are structurally derived from alkanes by substituting a hydrogen atom.

q: The replacement of one hydrogen atom in an alkane by a hydroxyl (OH) group gives the corresponding alcohol.
e: This substitution defines the basic structure of an alcohol.

q: Most of the common reactions of all alcohols are due to the functional group, OH.
e: The hydroxyl group is the reactive functional group responsible for alcohol chemistry.

q: They form a homologous series with the general formula $C_nH_{2n+1}OH$, where n is a number equal to or greater than 1.
e: The general formula for aliphatic alcohols is $C_nH_{2n+1}OH$.

q: The common name of an alcohol combines the name of the alkyl group with the word alcohol.
e: Common nomenclature uses the alkyl group name followed by 'alcohol'.

q: Alcohols are given their respective names by adding -ol instead of -e to the alkane.
e: IUPAC naming replaces the '-e' ending of the parent alkane with '-ol'.

q: The chain is numbered from the end nearest the OH group.
e: IUPAC rules prioritize giving the hydroxyl group the lowest possible locant.

q: Alcohols containing at least two carbon atoms have more than one structure.
e: Alcohols must contain at least three carbon atoms to exhibit structural isomerism.

q: Alcohols form chain isomerism due to the different structures of C-skeleton in the longer chain.
e: Chain isomers of alcohols have different carbon backbone arrangements.

q: The basic carbon skeleton remains unchanged in the isomers, but a hydroxyl group (OH) can be located in different positions, making them positional isomers.
e: Positional isomers differ only in the location of the functional group on the same carbon skeleton.

q: Ethene and steam are passed over a phosphoric acid catalyst at $570^{\circ} C$ and 60 ~ 70 atmospheric pressure to produce ethanol.
e: This is the industrial hydration method for producing ethanol from ethene.

q: This reaction is reversible; high pressure and a high temperature would give the best yield.
e: Because the reaction is exothermic, high pressure and a low temperature would give the best yield.

q: Starch is used as the raw material for the preparation of ethanol industrially.
e: Starchy materials like potatoes, maize, and rice are common raw materials for fermentation.

q: The cooked starch is cooled and then treated with freshly germinated barley which is called malt for 1 hour at $60^{\circ} C$.
e: Malt provides the enzyme diastase needed to break down starch.

q: Malt contains the enzyme diastase.
e: Diastase is the enzyme in malt that hydrolyzes starch into maltose.

q: Starch breaks down into a sugar called glucose.
e: Starch initially breaks down into a sugar called maltose, not directly into glucose.

q: Yeast secretes two enzymes: maltase which converts maltose into glucose and zymase which converts glucose into ethanol.
e: These two enzymes sequentially convert maltose to glucose and then glucose to ethanol and $CO_2$.

q: The product contains about 11% ethanol.
e: Fermentation naturally yields a dilute ethanol solution of about 11%.

q: It is fractionally distilled to yield the rectified spirit of commerce which contains about 95% ethanol.
e: Fractional distillation concentrates the ethanol to approximately 95%.

q: Alcohols from methanol to butanol are mobile liquids.
e: Lower alcohols are mobile liquids at room temperature.

q: The first two members; methanol and ethanol are miscible with water in any proportion.
e: Methanol and ethanol are completely miscible with water due to hydrogen bonding.

q: The most toxic member is ethanol.
e: The most toxic member of the lower alcohols is methanol, not ethanol.

q: When a piece of sodium is added to ethanol, reaction occurs at room temperature, liberating hydrogen.
e: Sodium reacts with alcohols to produce sodium alkoxide and hydrogen gas.

q: When ethanol is heated with an excess of concentrated sulphuric acid at $160^{\circ} C$, ethene is produced.
e: Dehydration of ethanol at $160^{\circ} C$ yields ethene.

q: With a smaller proportion of concentrated sulphuric acid, diethyl ether is formed when the reaction temperature is kept at $140^{\circ} C$.
e: Intermolecular dehydration at a lower temperature ($140^{\circ} C$) produces diethyl ether.

q: Ethanoic acid also reacts with ethanol when a small amount of concentrated sulphuric acid is added as catalyst.
e: This reaction is known as esterification.

q: Ethyl ethanoate is an ester.
e: The reaction between ethanoic acid and ethanol produces the ester ethyl ethanoate.

q: It has a pleasant fruity odour which is a characteristic of most esters.
e: Esters are well known for their characteristic pleasant, fruity smells.

q: When ethanol vapour is passed over freshly reduced copper heated at $300^{\circ} C$, removal of hydrogen occurs with formation of ethanal.
e: Catalytic dehydrogenation of ethanol yields ethanal (acetaldehyde).

q: When ethanol is heated with acidified potassium dichromate solution, oxidation takes place in two stages to finally give ethanoic acid.
e: Ethanol oxidizes first to ethanal and then to ethanoic acid.

q: Fermentation is a process in which ethanol is made from glucose using yeast in the presence of air.
e: Fermentation occurs in the absence of air (anaerobic conditions).

q: Esterification is a reaction of an alcohol with an acid to produce an ester and water.
e: Esterification is the condensation reaction between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid.

q: Dehydrogenation is a chemical reaction in which hydrogen is removed from a compound.
e: Dehydrogenation involves the loss of hydrogen atoms from a molecule.

q: Liquid alkanes have various effects on the body, depending on the part exposed.
e: The physiological effects of liquid alkanes vary based on the exposure site.

q: On the skin, alkanes dissolve body oils, and repeated contact may cause dermatitis.
e: Alkanes are nonpolar solvents that can strip natural oils from the skin.

q: Heavier liquid alkanes, when applied to the skin, act as emollients (skin softeners).
e: Heavier alkanes like petroleum jelly are used as protective emollients.

q: Ripening fruits and vegetables give off ethene, which triggers further ripening.
e: Ethene acts as a natural plant hormone that promotes ripening.

q: Ethyne is used as the fuel for the oxyacetylene blow lamp used in cutting and welding metals.
e: The high-temperature flame of oxyacetylene is ideal for metalworking.

q: Ethanol can be found in medical wipes and the most common antibacterial hand sanitiser gels as an antiseptic.
e: Ethanol is widely used for its antiseptic properties in healthcare and hygiene products.
